name: Surface Mount Technology

claims.claim_text: Through-hole construction is not disappearing. Open almost any modern consumer product and the power supply inside is a single-layer phenolic board with leaded parts, because that remains the cheapest way to build that particular thing.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a single-layer phenolic PCB with through-hole parts

claims.claim_text: Asked how long leaded parts will remain available, the working answer is decades rather than years. The demand is real and the parts are cheap and easy to produce, so nothing is forcing them out.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not years. It's decades

claims.claim_text: Vendors still ship new parts in dual in-line packages for two practical reasons: prototyping, and being able to pull a damaged device out of a socket and replace it immediately after a static discharge.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need to just switch it out real quick
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: There are designs where leaded parts win on specification rather than nostalgia. Surface-mount resistors have modest voltage ratings, around 300 volts even for the extended packages, which makes a several-hundred-volt supply awkward to build entirely in surface mount.
claims.quote_verbatim: a voltage rating for like a 0603 resistor. It's not that high

claims.claim_text: Choosing through-hole now means working against the process, because assembly houses are optimised for surface mount and you pay a premium for the exception. This is not symmetric with component size: a machine that places small passives places large ones just as easily, so going up in size costs nothing while going back to leads costs a process.
claims.quote_verbatim: if somebody's pick and place machine can, can do 0603, they can do 1206
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The economics that ended the kit era are stark. A board can be assembled at a local house for a couple of dollars, and kitting the same components into bags and labelling them costs more of your own time than that, quite apart from the customer's build time.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not worth a couple of bucks of your time to kit up the components
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Kits made sense historically because small-scale players had no access to manufacturing at all. Nobody would build a hundred boards for an individual, and everything was through-hole and therefore easy to handle by hand, so selling the parts was the only viable form.
claims.quote_verbatim: the manufacturing industry didn't exist for small scale players

claims.claim_text: Kits carry a negative cost through support. Selling a kit means supporting a kit, and a small business cannot afford the time that consumes, which is a separate consideration from whether the kit sells.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you sell kits, you have to support kits

claims.claim_text: A workable rule for whether something functions as a kit: if it takes more than about an hour for an average person to build, it probably does not, unless the act of building carries real value or the product is genuinely impossible to manufacture otherwise.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it takes more than an hour to build for an average person

claims.claim_text: Choosing through-hole purely to keep a product kittable is self-defeating, because it removes the cost advantage that was the argument for selling a kit in the first place. The modern answer for most products is surface mount and current parts, which may cost less outright.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're having to go through hole instead of surface mount just to keep it a kit

claims.claim_text: Surface-mount kits are unpleasant to assemble for reasons unrelated to soldering skill: components arrive cut from strips, and the passives carry no markings, so identifying what you are holding becomes the hard part.
claims.quote_verbatim: Surface mount kits are a pain in the ass

claims.claim_text: One response to that is to make the kit cheap enough that failure does not matter: a deliberately minimal surface-mount kit sold in a three-pack, so a beginner frightened of the process can destroy one without feeling bad about it.
claims.quote_verbatim: how can we make a kit as cheap as possible?
claims.speaker: Adam Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: The intimidation around surface mount rests on a false assumption. People imagine it must be done with a soldering iron, which is genuinely hard; shown solder paste methods instead, the same people find it easier than through-hole work.
claims.quote_verbatim: they think that must have been done with a soldering iron
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: The practice this points to is to use paste, a stencil and reflow almost exclusively for surface mount rather than hand soldering, even for one-off boards.
claims.quote_verbatim: I almost exclusively use solder paste and stencils and reflow
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Of the available assembly processes, surface mount is the forgiving one. Placement alignment has real tolerance and hot air reflow is straightforward, compared with trimming leads on through-hole parts and dealing with solder pots and wave equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: of all the processes, surface mount is very forgiving
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: The physical reason for that tolerance is surface tension. The parts are small and light enough that molten solder pulls them into alignment on their pads, so heating the board and letting the parts settle works, within limits.
claims.quote_verbatim: just the surface tension of the solder
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor

claims.claim_text: A hot plate holds temperature closely and has one advantage an oven cannot match: you can put a microscope over the board and watch the joints reflow. It struggles with tall components and large boards, where thermal gradients across the assembly become the problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually get your microscope on top of it and watch it while it's reflowing

claims.claim_text: The honest skill assessment is that surface mount is different rather than difficult. It needs a steady hand, tweezers and probably a microscope, and once learned it is straightforward work at an ordinary bench.
claims.quote_verbatim: It does require steady hand and a pair of tweezers and probably a microscope
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: Ball grid arrays are where the home or small-office line stops, because placement accuracy and X-ray inspection are both required and neither is available on a bench.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're not doing BGA there because you, then you need like x-ray

claims.claim_text: The process time asymmetry inside a real factory is worth internalising: a board passes through surface-mount assembly in about four and a half minutes, while trimming the leads on its through-hole parts before selective soldering takes around ten.
claims.quote_verbatim: that takes like 10 minutes. And the surface mount goes through in about four and a half minutes
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Selective soldering is how a mostly surface-mount board gets its few leaded parts attached without passing the whole assembly through a wave: a small nozzle of molten solder on an XY robot rises from below and solders each pin in turn.
claims.quote_verbatim: Selective solder is basically more like a, like a squirt gun of molten solder

claims.claim_text: That process imposes a layout rule. Keep surface-mount parts on the underside at least about ten millimetres away from through-hole pins, because otherwise the selective head cannot reach and those joints have to be hand soldered, which is where the cost appears.
claims.quote_verbatim: don't put your surface mount parts on the bottom of the board close to within like 10 millimeters of your through hole pins
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The design-phase consequence is that a single through-hole part brings an extra process step and keep-out areas that constrain the rest of the layout. That makes the question of whether the part is genuinely necessary worth asking before the board is laid out rather than after.
claims.quote_verbatim: does it really have to

claims.claim_text: The alternative to selective soldering is a shield masking whole sections of the board so it can pass through a wave, which is more expensive again. The ordering of options matters when deciding what a leaded connector actually costs.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not as expensive as like making a shield
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Some assembly services forbid through-hole outright as policy. Refusing the exception is what lets them run every job through one fixed process, which is where their price comes from.
claims.quote_verbatim: our policy on through-hole is that you can't have it
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: Low-cost assembly services publish a smallest acceptable passive size, often 0402, which sets a floor on the design before layout begins rather than after quoting.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think the smallest they'll do is 0402

claims.claim_text: Capability for the very smallest passives, 0201 and below, sits where phone volumes are, because that is what justifies the equipment. For genuinely cutting-edge process work, though, domestic suppliers can be easier to work with than distant ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have some pretty amazing stuff in terms of 0201
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller - Sudden SinoAmerican Synthesis

claims.claim_text: Cost reduction in a redesign came from shrinking the passives and merging individual resistors into arrays, because placement cost scales with the number of components rather than their value. Fewer, smaller parts is a cost decision more than a size one.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of the pick and place is related to the number of components

claims.claim_text: Surface-mount availability now drives which component types get chosen at all. Capacitor selection in particular is influenced by which technologies can be placed by machine, because avoiding a through-hole process entirely is worth a great deal.
claims.quote_verbatim: being able to avoid the through-hole process is important

claims.claim_text: The same effect appears part by part. A supercapacitor offered in a 1206 reflow-compatible package replaces a leaded round device and simply joins the existing placement run, which removes an entire process step from the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just drop it in as one of the other surface mount parts
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The quality bar in assembly is unforgiving. A prototype order may involve one or two thousand individual placements, and every one must be the right part in the right place in the right orientation, so a single dry joint spoils the order.
claims.quote_verbatim: every one of those has to go perfectly
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: A systems lesson from running an assembly operation: improving one process step does not improve the whole. Making surface mount ten times more efficient barely moved the overall system, because through-hole, reflow, selective soldering, hand assembly and inspection all remain in the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've saved made SMT like 10 X more efficient
claims.speaker: Andrew Seddon
claims.episode_title: CircuitHub, 12 Years Later with Andrew Seddon

claims.claim_text: The trap in bringing assembly in-house is that the placement machine is only the first purchase. A reflow oven and a stencil printer follow, and the machines themselves need constant attention both to get working initially and to keep working afterwards.
claims.quote_verbatim: these machines take a lot of babysitting
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vic Aprea - Federated Firmware Functionalism

claims.claim_text: The volume band that forces this decision is a genuinely bad one: several hundred to about a thousand units is too many to hand build and too few to attract good contract pricing, which is what pushes people into buying equipment they did not plan on.
claims.quote_verbatim: the prospect of soldering by hand, these fairly complex boards
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vic Aprea - Federated Firmware Functionalism

claims.claim_text: Placement itself is a solved automated problem rather than a frontier. What remains human is keeping finicky machines running, which is a maintenance role rather than an assembly one.
claims.quote_verbatim: assembly, that's totally done and dusted
claims.episode_title: FPGAs, Robots & Thermocouples - Wampum's Wavering Worth

claims.claim_text: Process variability concentrates wherever a liquid consumable is involved. Machine surface mount is remarkably consistent, while hand soldering and fed-solder processes vary much more, which is why the automated step is rarely the source of a yield problem.
claims.quote_verbatim: SMT is pretty darn close. They're really good at keeping that consistent

claims.claim_text: The way to get a factory to fix a defect is evidence rather than description. Saying something feels wrong achieves nothing, while a high-resolution photograph of a tombstoned component is acted on within the hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: a high res photo of a tombstone component is like gold

claims.claim_text: Co-locating surface-mount assembly with final assembly is worth arranging deliberately, because board-level problems are always discovered on the final assembly line and being able to walk between the two is what makes them fixable quickly.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're always going to find board level problems on a final assembly line

claims.claim_text: A cost-engineered module shows what optimising for assembly looks like: a two-layer board, single-sided surface mount, a simple power chain and a dual in-line form factor, all chosen so it is easy to automate, easy to package and usable as a component inside somebody else's product.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's single, you know, single side surface mount. Easy to automate
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: Mixing the two technologies on one connector is sometimes the point: combining through-hole and surface-mount attachment gives mechanical retention against shear forces that surface mount alone does not provide.
claims.quote_verbatim: we have this combination of through hole and surface mount that gives it the good retention
claims.speaker: Jason Kridner

claims.claim_text: Repairability follows from construction. Older equipment built with through-hole or large surface-mount parts, low clock speeds and five or three volt logic has no high-speed differential signalling, so a fault can usually be traced and fixed, or the missing function rebuilt with a small modern board.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're built with through-hole components or large-scale surface mount
claims.speaker: Trammell Hudson

claims.claim_text: An educational use of surface mount: an oversized working replica of a classic part, made in a surface-mount package with gull-wing leads at matched scale, specifically so people have something forgiving to practise the process on.
claims.quote_verbatim: we decided to build a surface mount version so that people could use that as a way to practice surface mount soldering
claims.speaker: Eric Schlaepfer
claims.episode_title: Open Circuits with Eric Schlaepfer and Windell Oskay

claims.claim_text: A physical constraint worth naming plainly: hand surface-mount work becomes impossible with a tremor. The work is demanding enough that a medical change can end it regardless of experience or skill.
claims.quote_verbatim: I just couldn't work surface mount anymore

claims.claim_text: The supply-chain reality behind moving assembly closer to home is unglamorous: when a line stops for a missing part, you cannot walk to a local market and buy a reel, because the component distribution that supports the line is where the manufacturing has been.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't just walk down the local markets and pick up a reel
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: One missing component stops the entire line regardless of how much of the bill of materials is available. Ninety percent of the parts in hand produces nothing at the end of a surface-mount line, which is why shortages hit assembly disproportionately.
claims.quote_verbatim: one part missing is no part out of the end of the service mount line
claims.speaker: Dave Young
